title: Visualizing the Recursion Call Stack Without Panic
excerpt: A calm, visual way to understand base cases, call frames, and how recursive functions build up and unwind on the stack.
lead: Recursion often feels like magic or a hall of mirrors. But inside your computer, it's just a stack of plates: each function call places a plate down, and returns pick plates back up one at a time.

sections.heading: 1. The Stack of Plates Metaphor
sections.body: When function `factorial(3)` calls `factorial(2)`, the computer cannot finish `factorial(3)` yet. It pauses, pushes a new memory frame onto the call stack for `factorial(2)`, and starts running that. Only when the top of the stack returns can lower frames resume.

sections.heading: 2. The Base Case Is the Floor
sections.body: Without a base case, your function stacks plates forever until memory runs out — causing the famous `RecursionError` or Stack Overflow. The base case is the condition where no further call is made; the recursion stops and starts returning values upward.

codeSnippet.caption: Base case terminates the chain at n=1

sections.heading: 3. The Two Phases: Winding & Unwinding
sections.body: Every recursive function goes through two distinct phases: Winding (calling deeper, passing parameters forward, building up the stack) and Unwinding (reaching the base case, calculating results, popping frames, and passing answers back).
sections.callout: Key insight: Work done before the recursive call happens on the way down; work done with the return value happens on the way up.

sections.heading: 4. Mental Model Checklist
sections.body: Before writing recursive code, answer three questions: 1. What is the smallest subproblem that can be answered immediately? (Base case) 2. How does each call make the input strictly smaller? 3. How do I combine the returned sub-result with current state?
